A B S T R A C T
Fall-from-height (FFH) accidents remain a leading cause of fatalities in the construction industry. To systemat
ically extract and analyze risk factors from unstructured FFH accident reports. this paper emploved large lan:
guage models (LLMs) to enable zero-shot automated fall-from-height knowledge graph (FFHKG) construction. By
clustering FFHKG entities to merge semantically similar factors, a weighted complex network is formed. enabling
topological analysis for quantitative risk assessment. A case study on 1097 FFH accident reports validates the
proposed framework. Results demonstrate that GPT-4o achieves high extraction accuracy, with an F1 score of
0.94 in named entity recognition and a precision of 0.90 in relationship extraction. Key risk factors, such as poor
safety management, lack of training, insufficient edge protection, etc., are quantitatively identified across
multiple perspectives. Observable unsafe behaviors are also detected, offering insights for behavior-based safety
monitoring. The proposed framework provides a data-driven solution for more effective safety management on
construction sites.

have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in processing and under
standing human language, significantly enhancing the efficiency of in
formation extraction [18]. LLMs offer a scalable solution for analyzing
vast amounts of unstructured accident reports, enabling the automated
construction of KG without relying on extensive labeled datasets. A
promising technique in this domain is prompt engineering, which op
timizes LLM output for downstream tasks without requiring model
retraining [19]. By formulating structured prompts, researchers can

flexibly and resource-efficiently. This approach reduces the dependence

different accident scenarios. Given the increasing complexity of risk

construction offers a powerful tool for advancing data-driven accident
analysis.
This paper aims to leverage LLMs to construct fall-from-height
knowledge graphs (FFHKG) from unstructured accident reports to
quantitatively analyze risk factors in FFH accidents. The main research
questions in this paper are: (1) How can structured knowledge be
accurately extracted from unstructured accident reports under a zero-
shot learning paradigm to construct a reliable FFHKG? (2) How can
the FFHKG be used to quantitatively analyze causal relationships and
identify key risk factors for FFH accidents? To solve these questions, this
paper first constructs the FFHKG automatically using LLMs. The entities
within the FFHKG are subsequently semantically embedded and
grouped using hierarchical clustering, enabling the fusion of similar
entities and the transformation of the FFHKG into a weighted complex
network that is easier to analyze. Topological analysis is then applied to
quantify the influence of each risk factor from different perspectives.
The novelty of this research lies in (a) developing a KG structure inte
grated with the AcciMap model, enabling a comprehensive representa
tion of multi-level causality in FFH accidents; (b) constructing a prompt-
based information extraction pipeline that enables zero-shot, LLM-
powered KG construction without the need for annotated training data;
(c) conducting a systematic and objective quantitative analysis of risk
factors through the networked causal structure extracted from a large
corpus of real-world accident reports.

comprehensively reviews existing studies on FFH accident factors
analysis and automated KG construction. Section 3 details the proposed
methodology. Section 4 reports the results of a case study of 1097 FFH
accidents, while Section 5 provides further discussion. Finally, Section 6
concludes the paper and outlines limitations and directions for future
research.

Understanding the underlying causes of FFH accidents and effec

improving construction safety. Therefore, this section reviews existing

pervision. For example, Luo et al. [20] utilized the Apriori algorithm to
examine 557 FFH accidents reported on construction sites from 2013 to
2019 and identified insufficient safety training and site complexity as
major contributing factors. Similarly, Nawi et al. [21] used question
naire data analyzed through a Likert scale and reported that inadequate
education and poor management were primary contributors to FFH
accidents. Equipment-related factors mainly include the absence or
improper use of personal protective equipment (PPE). Kang [22] con
ducted frequency analysis alongside chi-square and Kruskal–Wallis tests
on FFH accident data from 1997 to 2012, revealing that more than 70 %
of these accidents were linked to the absence of fall protection equip
ment. Cheng et al. [23] used data mining methods to investigate
construction-related occupational accidents in Taiwan and found that
the most commonly reported contributors to FFH accidents included
improper or missing PPE, insufficient safety awareness, and neglect of
hazard warnings. Environmental factors also play a crucial role in FFH
accidents. These include complex site layouts, adverse weather condi
tions. and deficiencies in safety installations such as guardrails and
scaffolding. Bobick [24] examined the Bureau of Labor Statistics from
1992 to 2000 and identified the absence of guardrails as a leading
contributor to FFH accidents. Halperin et al. [25] evaluated scaffold
safety at nine construction sites using a standardized checklist. high-
lighting missing planks, inadequate guardrails, and poor access as sig
nificant hazards. Individual factors primarily involve workers’ behavior,
experience, and risk perception. Wong et al. [26] reported that poor
safety attitudes and behaviors among workers posed major challenges to
construction site safety management. Jahangiri et al. [27] also found
that improper use of PPE and workers' neglect of protective measures
were common risk behaviors. In a study focused on the Malaysiar
construction sector, Ayob et al. [28] reported that 46.28 % of FFH ac

PPE, unsafe practices, and ineffective management.

thereby providing a scalable, data-driven framework for comprehensive

2.2. Automated knowledge graph construction
Building a comprehensive and efficient KG requires accurate infor
mation extraction to transform unstructured text into structured repre
sentations. However, accident reports are typically lengthy,
unstructured, and contain complex causal relationships, making high
precision and high-efficiency KG construction particularly challenging.
Some studies rely on manual extraction due to limited data availability,
but this approach is time-consuming, costly, and highly dependent on
subjective interpretation. As accident records grow, manual methods
become impractical for large-scale knowledge extraction.
To address these challenges, NLP techniques have been employed for
automated KG construction. Traditional KG construction involves
named entity recognition (NER) and relation extraction (RE) [34]. Gan
et al. [35] utilized NLP to extract textual information from maritime
accident reports, enabling structured KG queries to reveal accident
patterns. Wang et al. [36] tested convolutional neural network and
recurrent neural network models for relation extraction in construction
safety regulations, achieving an accuracy of 87.5 %. Chen et al. [13]
proposed a novel model based on a pre-trained language model for
water conservancy safety management, reaching over 85 % accuracy in
text recognition. While these studies demonstrate the potential of NLp
for KG construction, their effectiveness is highly dependent on large,
well-annotated datasets. These models perform well on training data but
often fail to generalize across different document formats and domains.
Moreover, accident reports vary in structure, covering diverse entities
related to people, behaviors, environments, and organizations. Unlike
general NLP tasks (e.g., extracting names and locations), KG construc
tion for accident analysis requires not only “recognition” but also deep
“understanding” of text content.
Given the limitations of traditional NLP models, LLMs offer a
promising alternative for KG construction. LLMs generate diverse out
puts based on prompts, making them highly adaptable for information
extraction tasks. Wei et al. [37] demonstrated that state-of-the-art LLMs
exhibit excellent zero-shot and few-shot extraction capabilities,
reducing dependence on large annotated datasets. Ashok et al. [38]
introduced Prompt-NER, which enhances entity recognition by
prompting LLMs to generate comprehensive lists of potential entities. In
a systematic evaluation, Li et al. [39] assessed GPT-3.5’s performance in
open information extraction but noted its limitations in handling com
plex relationship extraction tasks. Trajanoska et al. [40] proposed an
LLM-enhanced KG pipeline that integrates entity and relation extraction,
demonstrating improved performance in domain-specific knowledge
structuring. These findings suggest that LLMs can enhance KG con
struction efficiency and accuracy for accident analysis.
Despite LLMs’ potential, their application in the construction in
dustry remains at an early stage, particularly for unstructured accident
report analysis. Researchers have yet to systematically evaluate LLMs
performance in extracting construction-specific knowledge from un
structured texts. Current studies lack a comparative analysis of different
LLM architectures for accident-related IE tasks. Therefore, this paper
aims to develop an LLM-based prompt engineering approach to effi
ciently process large-scale unstructured accident reports, transforming
them into structured FFHKG components for comprehensive risk
assessment.
3. Methodology
This study develops an LLM-based framework for automated FFHKG
construction and quantitative analysis of risk factors from unstructured
accident reports. The overall workflow is illustrated in Fig. 1. First, the
KG ontology is established by adjusting the classical AcciMap model to
capture the hierarchical and causal structure of construction FFH acci
dents. Then, a prompt engineering strategy is introduced, combining
Prompt Chaining, Chain of Thought reasoning, and Self-Consistency
sampling to enable zero-shot information extraction for FFHKG gener
ation using LLMs. The entities of FFHKG are embedded into dense vec
tors and clustered using hierarchical agglomerative clustering to fuse
semantically similar nodes. The FFHKG is then transformed into a
weighted complex network that is more suitable for structural analysis.
Finally, topological analysis is applied to quantify the influence of each
factor from three perspectives: direct causality, indirect causality, and
accident risk propagation, providing a comprehensive understanding of
the key contributors to FFH accidents.
3.1. Construction of FFHKG ontology
KG is a structured representation of knowledge in the form of a se
mantic network, where entities, concepts, and events are linked through
meaningful relationships [41]. By embedding semantic metadata into
these connections, KG enables data integration, contextual under
standing, and advanced reasoning across heterogeneous sources.
Ontology provides the formal semantic foundation of KG, defining the
types of entities, their attributes, and relationships. As the schema of the
graph, ontology ensures consistent interpretation and semantic inter
operability across domains.
In the domain of construction safety, KGs offer a promising tool to
systematically capture complex causality of accidents. Accident reports
often contain detailed but unstructured descriptions of unsafe behaviors,
faulty equipment, and organizational failures. To support automated
knowledge extraction and causal reasoning in this context, a domain
specific ontology is needed to represent the hierarchical structure and
interactions among multiple facilities, personnel, and management
layers. To achieve this, the AcciMap framework is adopted as the
foundation for constructing the FFHKG ontology. Originally proposed by
Rasmussen, AcciMap is designed to identify failures, decisions, and ac
tions across different levels of a socio-technical system and to analyze
the interactions among these elements that lead to accidents [42]. As

their interactions as edges. This enables the application of network
metrics (e.g., centrality, clustering coefficient) to evaluate the impor
tance and connectivity of risk factors [33]. Given that KG inherently
possesses a network structure, it offers an ideal platform to integrate
SAA-based classifications with quantitative causal inference. Although
complex network theory has been successfully applied in accident
analysis in other domains [12,33], it has not yet been widely imple
mented in the context of FFH risk analysis. Therefore, this paper pro
poses a method for constructing an automated FFHKG grounded in the
AcciMap model. By applying network analysis techniques to FFHKG, we
aim to quantify the strength of causal relationships among risk factors,
thereby providing a scalable, data-driven framework for comprehensive
FFH risk assessment.
2.2. Automated knowledge graph construction
Building a comprehensive and efficient KG requires accurate infor
mation extraction to transform unstructured text into structured repre
sentations. However, accident reports are typically lengthy,
unstructured, and contain complex causal relationships, making high
precision and high-efficiency KG construction particularly challenging.
Some studies rely on manual extraction due to limited data availability,
but this approach is time-consuming, costly, and highly dependent on
subjective interpretation. As accident records grow, manual methods
become impractical for large-scale knowledge extraction.
To address these challenges, NLP techniques have been employed for
automated KG construction. Traditional KG construction involves
named entity recognition (NER) and relation extraction (RE) [34]. Gan
et al. [35] utilized NLP to extract textual information from maritime
accident reports, enabling structured KG queries to reveal accident
patterns. Wang et al. [36] tested convolutional neural network and
recurrent neural network models for relation extraction in construction
safety regulations, achieving an accuracy of 87.5 %. Chen et al. [13]
proposed a novel model based on a pre-trained language model for
water conservancy safety management, reaching over 85 % accuracy in
text recognition. While these studies demonstrate the potential of NLp
for KG construction, their effectiveness is highly dependent on large,
well-annotated datasets. These models perform well on training data but
often fail to generalize across different document formats and domains.
Moreover, accident reports vary in structure, covering diverse entities
related to people, behaviors, environments, and organizations. Unlike
general NLP tasks (e.g., extracting names and locations), KG construc
tion for accident analysis requires not only “recognition” but also deep
“understanding” of text content.
Given the limitations of traditional NLP models, LLMs offer a
promising alternative for KG construction. LLMs generate diverse out
puts based on prompts, making them highly adaptable for information
extraction tasks. Wei et al. [37] demonstrated that state-of-the-art LLMs
exhibit excellent zero-shot and few-shot extraction capabilities,
reducing dependence on large annotated datasets. Ashok et al. [38]
introduced Prompt-NER, which enhances entity recognition by
prompting LLMs to generate comprehensive lists of potential entities. In
a systematic evaluation, Li et al. [39] assessed GPT-3.5’s performance in
open information extraction but noted its limitations in handling com
plex relationship extraction tasks. Trajanoska et al. [40] proposed an
LLM-enhanced KG pipeline that integrates entity and relation extraction,
demonstrating improved performance in domain-specific knowledge
structuring. These findings suggest that LLMs can enhance KG con
struction efficiency and accuracy for accident analysis.
Despite LLMs’ potential, their application in the construction in
dustry remains at an early stage, particularly for unstructured accident
report analysis. Researchers have yet to systematically evaluate LLMs
performance in extracting construction-specific knowledge from un
structured texts. Current studies lack a comparative analysis of different
LLM architectures for accident-related IE tasks. Therefore, this paper
aims to develop an LLM-based prompt engineering approach to effi
ciently process large-scale unstructured accident reports, transforming
them into structured FFHKG components for comprehensive risk
assessment.
3. Methodology
This study develops an LLM-based framework for automated FFHKG
construction and quantitative analysis of risk factors from unstructured
accident reports. The overall workflow is illustrated in Fig. 1. First, the
KG ontology is established by adjusting the classical AcciMap model to
capture the hierarchical and causal structure of construction FFH acci
dents. Then, a prompt engineering strategy is introduced, combining
Prompt Chaining, Chain of Thought reasoning, and Self-Consistency
sampling to enable zero-shot information extraction for FFHKG gener
ation using LLMs. The entities of FFHKG are embedded into dense vec
tors and clustered using hierarchical agglomerative clustering to fuse
semantically similar nodes. The FFHKG is then transformed into a
weighted complex network that is more suitable for structural analysis.
Finally, topological analysis is applied to quantify the influence of each
factor from three perspectives: direct causality, indirect causality, and
accident risk propagation, providing a comprehensive understanding of
the key contributors to FFH accidents.
3.1. Construction of FFHKG ontology
KG is a structured representation of knowledge in the form of a se
mantic network, where entities, concepts, and events are linked through
meaningful relationships [41]. By embedding semantic metadata into
these connections, KG enables data integration, contextual under
standing, and advanced reasoning across heterogeneous sources.
Ontology provides the formal semantic foundation of KG, defining the
types of entities, their attributes, and relationships. As the schema of the
graph, ontology ensures consistent interpretation and semantic inter
operability across domains.
In the domain of construction safety, KGs offer a promising tool to
systematically capture complex causality of accidents. Accident reports
often contain detailed but unstructured descriptions of unsafe behaviors,
faulty equipment, and organizational failures. To support automated
knowledge extraction and causal reasoning in this context, a domain
specific ontology is needed to represent the hierarchical structure and
interactions among multiple facilities, personnel, and management
layers. To achieve this, the AcciMap framework is adopted as the
foundation for constructing the FFHKG ontology. Originally proposed by
Rasmussen, AcciMap is designed to identify failures, decisions, and ac
tions across different levels of a socio-technical system and to analyze
the interactions among these elements that lead to accidents [42]. As
illustrated in Fig. 2(a), the original AcciMap framework comprises six
hierarchical levels aligned with risk management structures. This hier
archical structure allows both bottom-up classification and top-down
causality tracing, making it well-suited for modeling accident causation
in construction sites [43].

original fifth level has been divided into Individual Activities and Ac

specific to FFH accidents.

3.2.3. Evaluation of extraction performance
Assessing the accuracy of entities and relationships extracted by
LLMs is essential to ensure the reliability and practical value of the
FFHKG. Human expertise plays a crucial role in evaluating the quality
and correctness of the extracted information and in identifying relevant
entities that may have been missed. Therefore, manual annotation by
domain experts is employed as the reference standard. For entity eval
uation, experts first determine whether the extracted entity is mentioned
in the report and whether its type is correctly identified. They also
annotate any relevant entities present in the report that were not
extracted by the model. For relationships, experts assess whether the
linked entities are accurate and whether the relation is appropriately
expressed in the report. To minimize subjective bias, multiple experts
independently evaluate each extraction. Inter-annotator agreement is
quantified using Fleiss’ Kappa, which statistically measures the consis
tency among annotators and ensures the reliability of the reference
standard [46]. Only the annotations that meet the agreement threshold
are used as the final reference standard for subsequent performance
evaluation.
This study employs well-known metrics to assess the quality of the
extracted entities and relationships. The extraction quality of both en
tities and entity relationships will be evaluated separately. We first use
the classic confusion matrix entries to evaluate the performance of
extracting each component. Specifically, correctly extracted
components are considered True Positives (TP), while incorrect ones are
labeled as False Positives (FP), and missing entities are treated as False
Negatives (FN). Based on these classifications, Precision (P) is computed
as the ratio of correct results to all retrieved results, and Recall (R) is the
ratio of correct results to all relevant results. The F1 score, defined as the
harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, provides a balanced evaluation
of both metrics.

Accident reports are unstructured texts, and the expressions of
various entities may be inconsistent. For instance, entities such as

network. Therefore, it is necessary to fuse knowledge by merging mul

4. Case study
To validate the effectiveness and applicability of the proposed
methodology, this section presents a case study based on real-world FFH
accident data. A large-scale dataset of construction site FFH accident
reports was collected and analyzed. The FFHKG was automatically
constructed using LLMs and subsequently refined into a complex
network to enable quantitative analysis of risk factors.
4.1. Data collection
To construct the database for construction site FFH accidents. this
study collected a total of 4590 accident cases using web crawlers. The
detailed accident reports were obtained from the “Safety Production
Management” section on the official websites of various provincial and
municipal governments in China. Additionally, using search engines on
government websites, keywords such as “fall-from-height accidents,”
“accident reports,” and “accident investigations” were employed to
search for accident cases directly. After thorough filtering, 1097 acci
dent cases were retained for the dataset in this study. The filtering
process followed two main principles: (1) Only accidents with detailed
reports, including direct and indirect causes, were retained. Many cases
were recorded on websites with minimal information, making it difficult
to extract risk factors. These cases were excluded from the dataset. (2)
Only accidents in the past ten years were selected. Earlier data may not
accurately reflect the current state of safety management on construc
tion sites, as it may lack recent updates and safety practices. Therefore,
accidents from 2014 to 2023 were chosen. Additionally, many accident
reports are removed from government websites after some time, so the
reports collected in this study represent all available reports from 2014
to 2023. While the 1097 cases are not the total number of FFH accidents
in China during this period, they contain detailed information useful for
further analysis. All reports were converted into .txt format for unifor
mity in data processing.

4.2.1. Extraction results of FFHKG
In this study, a prompt-based approach was implemented using
LLMs. Using the constructed prompts, knowledge entities and relation
ships can be sequentially identified. Different LLMs exhibit varying
performance in causal reasoning, long-text comprehension, and
computational efficiency. To identify the most suitable LLM for knowl
edge extraction, we conducted a comparative evaluation of six leading
LLMs.
We selected GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet as
representatives of closed-source LLMs. These closed-source models
exhibit strong overall performance due to high-quality pretraining data
and carefully optimized architectures. GPT-4o is known for its robust
generalization and ability to reason in context. Claude 3.7 Sonnet,
focusing on interpretability and instruction alignment, performs stably
in structured extraction tasks. Gemini 2.0 Flash offers exceptional speed
and cost efficiency, making it attractive for large-scale batch processing.
In contrast, open-source models offer greater flexibility, transparency,
and local deployment potential. For this category, we included Llama
3.3, Qwen 2.5, and DeepSeek R1. Qwen 2.5 is optimized for Chinese
content understanding, making it particularly suitable for Chinese-
language accident reports. DeepSeek R1, on the other hand, represents
a model with strong reasoning abilities, especially in multi-hop tasks.
Three experts were invited to manually annotate a random sample of
100 accident reports to assess the extraction accuracy. The inter-
annotator agreement was evaluated using Fleiss’ Kappa, resulting in a
coefficient of 0.927, which indicates almost perfect agreement. This
high consistency validates the reliability of the expert-annotated refer
ence standard used for performance evaluation. The final evaluation
metrics were calculated based on the average value of the three experts.

In the organizational domain, inadequate safety management,
insufficient hazard identification, and lack of safety training emerged as
dominant contributors, aligning with existing findings [28,30,51,52].
Notably, the inadequate safety education of the contractor and sub
contractor exhibits significantly higher risk values than other risk fac
tors. Future projects should enhance the accessibility and effectiveness
of safety education while fostering proactive worker participation,
which is critical for sustained behavioral change. Although construction
owners are not directly involved in site operations, their decisions
significantly shape upstream risk structures. Strengthening safety
awareness training for owners can create a top-down safety culture,
influencing supervisors, contractors, and subcontractors.
In terms of equipment safety, failure to wear safety harnesses and
helmets are the most critical risk factors, issues that have been widely
discussed in existing academic research [53,54]. Regarding environ
mental safety, insufficient edge protection and inadequate hole protec
tion are identified as primary hazards, consistent with the existing
conclusions [55,56]. These findings validate the effectiveness of the
methodology proposed in this study. Unlike traditional approaches that
rely on expert judgment, this research derives data-driven insights from
a large dataset of historical accident reports, ensuring the robustness of
its conclusions. Frequent references to safety management deficiencies
and inadequate hazard detection indicate that site supervision solely
reliant on designated personnel is insufficient. Once unsafe behaviors
occur, they may rapidly escalate into serious accidents. Therefore, safety
monitoring should be enhanced through a combination of automated
equipment inspection, environmental optimization, and AI-based
violation detection to interrupt accident development paths.
Additionally, since accident reports primarily document observable
unsafe behaviors, this study points to positional shifts, climbing activ
ities, and demolition operations as key contributing factors. In contrast,
some research places greater emphasis on workers’ personal safety
habits and risk perception [57,58], highlighting a difference in research
focus that complements the findings of this study. By focusing on
observable actions and accident status, the results of this study offer
additional insights into actionable risk mitigation. Among all unsafe
actions, climbing-related activities pose the highest risk. This suggests
that future posture recognition systems for high-altitude operations
should prioritize the detection of climbing motions to enable timely
warnings and interventions. Finally, demolition work was found to carry
the highest overall risk among task types, likely due to unstable struc
tures and dynamic environments. Enhanced supervision and targeted
protective measures are essential for workers performing demolition at
heights.

refined AcciMap-based ontology, prompt engineering strategies, and
network-based topology metrics, the proposed method enables robust
extraction of structured causal information from unstructured accident
reports and supports comprehensive, data-driven risk factor quantitative
evaluation.
